area: Area V. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can work out an approximate pivotal altitude from groundspeed and pylon elevation, explain why groundspeed (not bank) sets it, and fly a coordinated eight on pylons that keeps the line of sight on each pylon with the bank never past 40°.
why: Eights on pylons is the most advanced and difficult ground reference maneuver, and the AFH says nothing beats it for building intuitive control of the airplane [[24:160|AFH 7-14]]. It is flown low, turning, with your eyes outside on a point on the ground, which is exactly where uncoordinated flight, distraction and obstacles cause accidents [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

prereading.what: Eights on pylons: line of sight, pivotal altitude rule of thumb, too high and too low, pylon selection, entry, corrections and common errors. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 7-14 to 7-18

warmup: Think first: you circle a grain bin with a 30° bank and it seems to slide forward along the wing. You steepen to 40° and it still slides. Then you climb 150 feet and it stops dead on your sight line. Why would height fix what bank could not?

key_terms.def: A ground reference maneuver in which you fly a figure eight around two points on the ground and vary altitude to keep a sight line pivoting on each point [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].
A prominent point on the ground that the airplane turns around. Good pylons are easy to see, at the same elevation and on a line perpendicular to the wind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
The altitude at which, for a given groundspeed, the projected sight line to a point on the ground appears to pivot on that point [[24:383|AFH G-11]] [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
An imaginary line from your eyes to the pylon, parallel to the airplane's lateral axis. It is not necessarily the wingtip [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].
Speed over the ground. Headed upwind it is less than airspeed; headed downwind it is more [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].
Sideways movement over the ground caused by wind. Doubling your speed does not change how fast the wind moves you sideways [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Angling the nose into the wind just enough to cancel drift so you track straight over the ground [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Rudder applied with aileron to cancel adverse yaw so the airplane turns without slipping or skidding [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
Uncoordinated flight. In a skid you feel pressed toward the outside of the turn; in a slip, toward the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other. It can come with little warning and roll the airplane toward inverted, often the start of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
An aggravated stall with autorotation. It needs a stall plus yaw; a stall in a slipping or skidding turn can start one [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
Planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed as the airplane's stored energy [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

chunks.title: Eights on pylons at commercial standards

body.p: Eights on pylons is a figure eight flown around two points on the ground, the pylons. Unlike eights around pylons, you change altitude to keep a fixed sight line to each pivot point. The AFH calls it the most advanced and difficult ground reference maneuver and says it is unmatched for developing intuitive control of the airplane [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

Its purpose: in earlier ground track maneuvers you fly a set path over the ground and correct for wind. Here you hold your lateral orientation to one spot, which builds the ability to fly accurately while dividing attention between the flightpath and the pylons [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS skill element
rows: Determine the approximate pivotal altitude (ACS CA.V.E.S2)
Select suitable pylons that permits straight-and-level flight between the pylons (ACS CA.V.E.S3)
Enter the maneuver in the correct direction and position using an appropriate altitude and airspeed (ACS CA.V.E.S4)
Establish the correct bank angle for the conditions, not to exceed 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5)
Apply smooth and continuous corrections so that the line-of-sight reference line remains on the pylon (ACS CA.V.E.S6)
Divide attention between accurate, coordinated airplane control and outside visual references (ACS CA.V.E.S7)
Maintain pylon position using appropriate pivotal altitude, avoiding slips and skids (ACS CA.V.E.S8)

body.p: Notice what is not there: no altitude or airspeed tolerance in feet or knots. The one hard number is the 40° bank limit. The examiner judges whether the sight line stays on the pylon, whether you stay coordinated, and whether you keep your head outside.

callout.text: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant, the evaluator must select Eights on Pylons, together with Steep Turns or Steep Spiral and Chandelles or Lazy Eights (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). There is no choosing around it.

check.q: What is the only numeric limit in the commercial ACS skill elements for this Task?
check.a: Bank: correct for the conditions, not to exceed 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5).

chunks.title: The line of sight: your reference to the pylon

body.p: Picture a taut string from your eyes to the pylon. The goal is to keep that string parallel to the airplane's lateral axis all the way around the pylon, never angled forward or back. Along that line the airplane appears to pivot on the pylon [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

Some instructors call this 'the wingtip on the pylon'. The AFH says that is not correct. High-wing, low-wing, swept and tapered wings, and tandem or side-by-side seats all give different angles from the eye to the wingtip. The sight line may sit ahead of, behind, above or below the wingtip, and it differs for each pilot and seat. In side-by-side airplanes it varies little if the two pilots' eyes are at about the same level [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].
The two photos in the figure show the result when you are off the pivotal altitude: too high, and the pylon sits ahead of your sight line; too low, and the pylon sits behind it [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

callout.text: Application: on the ground, sit at your normal seat height and find a mark on the wing, strut or window frame that lies on a line parallel to the lateral axis from your eyes. Use that mark in the air, and re-find it if you change seats or seat height [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

check.q: Why does 'put the wingtip on the pylon' fail as a definition?
check.a: Wing shape and seat position change the angle from the eye to the wingtip. The real reference is an eye-level line parallel to the lateral axis [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

chunks.title: Pivotal altitude and the rule of thumb

body.p: The right altitude for eights on pylons is the pivotal altitude, and it is set by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. At that altitude, for a given groundspeed, the sight line projected to the pylon appears to pivot on it [[24:383|AFH G-11]].

bullets: Groundspeed in knots: square it and divide by 11.3 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
Groundspeed in miles per hour: square it and divide by 15 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
Then add the MSL elevation of the pylon to get the altitude to fly [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

body.p: The table's numbers are heights above the pylon, rounded. Check one: 100 knots x 100 knots = 10,000, and 10,000 / 11.3 = 885 feet, as the table shows [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
Worked example: pylons on ground at 620 feet MSL, groundspeed 95 knots. 95 x 95 = 9,025. 9,025 / 11.3 = 799 feet above the pylon. 799 + 620 = about 1,419 feet MSL on the altimeter.

Do this in preflight planning. Get wind direction and speed from weather reports or other pilots in the area, the pylons' MSL elevation from the sectional chart, and the range of maneuvering airspeeds (by weight) from the POH. Work out a pivotal altitude for each position: upwind, downwind and crosswind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

callout.text: Groundspeed squared, over 11.3 for knots or 15 for mph, plus the pylon's elevation.
The number is only a starting point. In the air you find the pivotal altitude by watching the sight line; trying to correct it by the altimeter does not work [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

check.q: Groundspeed 100 knots, pylon at 1,000 feet MSL. About what should the altimeter read?
check.a: 100 x 100 / 11.3 = 885 feet above the pylon, plus 1,000 = about 1,885 feet MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

chunks.title: Why groundspeed sets it and bank does not

body.p: The pivotal altitude does not change with bank angle unless the bank is steep enough to change the groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. The bank you choose does not alter it [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. What the bank does depend on is your distance from the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

In the figure, three airplanes sit at the same pivotal altitude with 60°, 45° and 30° of bank. The closer one is to the pylon, the steeper its bank. That is why an instructor can ask you to enter at a distance that gives a chosen bank at the steepest point of the turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Application, why 11.3: the PHAK gives turn radius in feet as speed in knots squared / (11.26 x tan bank) [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]]. For the sight line along the lateral axis to hit the pylon at the center of the turn, height = radius x tan bank. Put the two together and tan bank cancels: height = speed squared / 11.26, which rounds to the AFH's 11.3. Bank drops out, so only speed sets the height; the AFH rule uses groundspeed because that is what you see over the ground.

callout.text: Application: at 885 feet above the pylon, a 40° bank needs a radius of 885 / tan 40° = 885 / 0.839 = about 1,055 feet. Fly closer than that and the bank goes past the ACS limit, so judge your entry distance with the 40° cap in mind (ACS CA.V.E.S5).

check.q: You fly closer to the pylon at the same groundspeed. What changes: the pivotal altitude or the bank?
check.a: The bank gets steeper; the pivotal altitude stays the same [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Too high or too low: reading the pylon

body.p: Above the pivotal altitude the projected sight line seems to move rearward in a circle relative to the pylon. Below it, the sight line seems to move forward [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

bullets: The AFH demonstration: at maneuvering speed and below pivotal altitude, roll into a medium bank. The sight line moves forward along the ground and the pylon appears to move back [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Climb well above pivotal altitude, back to maneuvering speed, medium bank again. Now the sight line moves backward across the ground and the pylon appears to move forward [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Reduce power and descend at maneuvering speed in the continuing turn. The backward motion slows, then stops for an instant. That altitude is the pivotal altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
If you sink below it, add power to hold airspeed while you regain altitude until the line pivots on the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

head: What you see
Meaning
Fix
rows: Sight line moves ahead of the pylon (pylon appears to move back)
Sight line moves behind the pylon (pylon appears to move ahead)

callout.text: Pylon runs ahead: you are high, come down. Pylon falls behind: you are low, go up. Figure 7-11 labels it the same way [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

For short blips from gusts or inattention: shallow the bank a little and fly nearly straight to bring a lagging sight line forward, or steepen it briefly to turn back a sight line that has moved ahead. With practice these fixes become barely visible [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

check.q: Halfway around, the pylon seems to slide ahead of your sight line. Climb or descend?
check.a: Descend. Pylon ahead means you are above the pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]] [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

chunks.title: Wind, groundspeed and the ground track

body.p: Wind moves the whole air mass. At 90 knots with a 10-knot wind from the right, you drift left 10 nautical miles every hour; double your speed to 180 knots and you still drift 10 nautical miles an hour [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

Wind also changes groundspeed. Headed upwind, groundspeed is less than airspeed; headed downwind, it is more. The effect is biggest when the wind is along the longitudinal axis and smallest when it is straight across [[24:149|AFH 7-3]].

Hold one bank angle in wind and the turn over the ground stretches: the radius grows where groundspeed is high and shrinks where it is low [[24:149|AFH 7-3]]. In constant-radius maneuvers you vary the bank to fix that [[24:149|AFH 7-3]] [[24:150|AFH 7-4]]. Eights on pylons is different: the turn does not have to be a constant radius, so you do not apply drift correction in the turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Between the pylons, though, you do need a wind correction angle [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Because your heading keeps swinging between downwind and upwind, groundspeed keeps changing, so the pivotal altitude changes through the turn. Climb or descend as needed to hold the sight line on the pylon [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Headed upwind, groundspeed drops, the pivotal altitude drops, and you descend [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Table: application of the rule of thumb [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. You are never on the pylon heading straight downwind, so the real spread in a pylon turn is smaller, but the direction is the lesson: faster over the ground, higher; slower, lower.

check.q: Why do you not fly a wind correction angle while turning around the pylon?
check.a: The pylon turn does not have to be a constant radius; you hold the sight line with altitude instead [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Choosing pylons and the practice area

body.p: Good pylons make the maneuver; poor pylon choice is on the AFH error list [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

bullets: Prominent enough to find again as you finish one turn and head for the next [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
Spaced so the straight-and-level leg between turns lasts 3 to 5 seconds: enough time to plan, not so much that you fly long straight legs [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
At the same elevation; a difference of more than a few feet means climbing or descending between turns [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
On a line perpendicular to the wind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

body.p: The area matters as much as the pylons. Stay well away from open air assemblies of people, congested areas and herds of livestock. Look for other aircraft, including helicopters, and for towers and wires. Have one or more emergency landing spots in mind [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

bullets: Ground reference maneuvers are generally flown between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL, with at least 500 feet of vertical and 2,000 feet of horizontal clearance from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Over other than congested areas: 500 feet above the surface; over sparsely populated areas, no closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].
Over congested areas: 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within 2,000 feet [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].
Anywhere: high enough for an emergency landing without undue hazard to people or property if the engine quits [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

callout.text: Application: a farmhouse or barn is a tempting pylon, but you will circle it for minutes at a few hundred feet of slant range. Check the 500-foot rule and the people and animals around it before you pick it [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
Many instructors already have pylons picked for the practice area, which lets you look up their elevation on the sectional before the flight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

check.q: Your favorite pylon is a lone barn in sparsely populated farmland. Which rule do you check first?
check.a: No closer than 500 feet to any person, vessel, vehicle or structure [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

chunks.title: Flying the eight: entry to recovery

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH gives the airspeed; the ACS asks for an appropriate altitude and airspeed at entry (ACS CA.V.E.S4).

bullets: 1. Complete the checklist, announce on the practice area frequency, and clear the area with two 90° clearing turns, looking left, right, above and below [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

2. Level at the approximate pivotal altitude for the crosswind legs. The AFH demonstration uses maneuvering speed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]], and its general guidance is not to exceed maneuvering speed in ground reference maneuvers [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].
3. Fly diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind of the first pylon, so the first turn is made into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
4. As the pylon appears just ahead of the wingtip, roll in by lowering the upwind wing until the sight line lies on the pylon [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
5. Heading upwind, groundspeed falls and so does the pivotal altitude: descend to hold the line [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
6. Turning toward downwind, groundspeed builds: expect to climb. Figure 7-10 marks this part 'gaining altitude' [[24:160|AFH 7-14]] [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].
7. Roll out toward a downwind heading and fly diagonally, with a wind correction angle, to a point downwind of the second pylon as far from it as you started from the first [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
8. Turn the opposite way around the second pylon, flying it the same way [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

body.p: Recovery: the AFH does not describe one. Application: when the examiner calls it, roll out on a straight leg between the pylons, return to cruise power and a safe altitude, and keep scanning.

callout.text: Bank: correct for the conditions, never more than 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5). If a turn needs more, the AFH says exit and set up again farther from the reference [[24:151|AFH 7-5]].
Clear, diagonal in, downwind of the pylon, roll in, down going upwind, up going downwind, diagonal out, other way.

check.q: Where are you, relative to the first pylon, when you roll into the first turn?
check.a: Downwind of it, so the first turn is into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Hold the pylon with altitude, not rudder

body.p: The most common error is using rudder to hold the pylon. When the sight line moves forward of the pylon, many pilots push inside rudder to yaw the wing back; when it moves behind, they push outside rudder to yaw it forward. Use the rudder only for coordination [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].
Yawing the wing onto the pylon puts the airplane in uncoordinated flight, at low altitude, in a steep bank, and should not be attempted [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

Coordination means rudder with the aileron to cancel adverse yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. In a skid you feel pushed to the outside of the turn; in a slip, to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Holding uncoordinated control deflections creates the potential for a spin, especially at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

bullets: Inside rudder to drag the wing back is a skid. A skidding cross-control stall can roll the airplane toward inverted with little warning [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can start a spin in the direction of the rudder, whichever wing is high [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].
If a stall happens in the turn: reduce the angle of attack until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Pylon errors are altitude errors. Fix them with pitch and power. Feet are for the ball.

check.q: The sight line runs ahead of the pylon and you feel pressed to the outside of the turn. What did you do and what should you do?
check.a: You pushed inside rudder and skidded [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Center the ball and climb, because the line ahead of the pylon means you are low [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

chunks.title: Low altitude: stall, spin, CFIT and energy

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers put you in a low-altitude environment with its own hazards [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Mismanaged altitude and airspeed feed the most common fatal accident types: loss of control in flight, controlled flight into terrain (CFIT), and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

Stall margin: in preflight planning, find the POH stall speed at 50° or at the steepest bank you expect, so you know your margin [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Application: at the 40° limit the load factor is 1 / cos 40° = 1.31, and its square root is 1.14, so an airplane that stalls at 50 knots wings level stalls at about 57 knots.

Energy: you change altitude all through this maneuver. Trading airspeed for altitude, or the reverse, moves them in opposite directions unless you change thrust [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. So the AFH has you reduce power to descend at maneuvering speed and add power to climb while holding airspeed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

bullets: Your energy picture is indicated altitude and indicated airspeed, not height above the ground or groundspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

The lower you fly, the faster the airplane seems to move over the ground [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Application: on the downwind side the ground rushes past; check the airspeed indicator before you decide you are fast.
Application: a climb with no added power bleeds airspeed, which lowers groundspeed, which lowers the pivotal altitude you were climbing toward. Use power, not just pitch.

body.p: CFIT: look for towers and wires, keep 500 feet of vertical and 2,000 feet of horizontal clearance from obstructions [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and remember that your altitude target moves with groundspeed, so check the obstacles under the whole eight, not just the pylons.

callout.text: Low, turning and looking down at a pylon is the setup for a stall-spin with no room to recover. Keep the ball centered, the bank at or under 40°, and the airspeed where you planned it (ACS CA.V.E.S5) [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

check.q: You climb toward the downwind pivotal altitude with pitch alone. What happens to airspeed, and why does it matter here?
check.a: Airspeed drops as altitude rises [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. Lower airspeed means less stall margin and a lower groundspeed; add power to hold airspeed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

chunks.title: Clearing, traffic and emergency landing options

body.p: Clear the area with two 90° clearing turns, looking left, right, above and below. Look for other aircraft, including helicopters, and announce on a practice area frequency if one is used [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Failing to clear the area 'initially and throughout the maneuver' tops the AFH error list [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

bullets: Scan in short, regular eye movements of no more than 10°, holding each for at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
During training, say the clearing out loud: 'clear left, right, above, and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
A target with no relative motion that only grows larger is on a collision course; take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Wings and door posts hide traffic. Move your head, and sometimes lift a wing, to look [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Haze, dust, smoke and flying toward the sun cut how well you can see targets [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: Application: in this maneuver your eyes spend long stretches on a point on the ground off one wing. Make the 3 to 5 second straight leg between pylons a traffic check, and glance up and out at every pylon.

Emergency landing: before you enter, have one or more landing spots; at low altitude you have less time to configure and less glide distance if the engine quits [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. If it does, establish best glide speed [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. You already know the wind, since your pylons sit across it [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Landing into it helps: doubling groundspeed means four times the destructive energy at touchdown [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

callout.text: Application: name your forced landing field out loud before the first pylon turn, and pick one you could reach from either pylon.

check.q: Why does landing into the wind matter so much in a forced landing from an eight on pylons?
check.a: It lowers groundspeed, and the destructive energy goes with the square of groundspeed: double it and you get four times the energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].

chunks.title: Division of attention and staying oriented

body.p: Ground reference maneuvers train division of attention. You control attitude while tracking a path over the ground, scan for hazards such as other aircraft, stay ready for an emergency landing, and check the flight and engine instruments at regular intervals so something like falling oil pressure does not catch you by surprise [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].
Do not fixate. A pilot staring at one reference loses the ability to judge rate. Scan across several references to see closure and drift [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

bullets: Situational awareness includes the airplane's position, its flightpath, other aircraft in the area, the environment, and the human factors in play [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].
It lets you plan what comes next and spot a deviation early [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Application: know which pylon is next and which way you will turn before you roll out.
An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn can cause the Coriolis illusion, the most overwhelming illusion in flight. Avoid sudden, extreme head movements [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
Failing to maintain orientation and to assess wind direction are listed errors for eights around pylons, the companion maneuver, and they apply here too [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

callout.text: Application: task priority while turning is airplane control first (attitude, ball, airspeed), then the pylon, then the next pylon and traffic. A radio call or a question can wait for the straight leg between pylons.

If you lose the pylon or get disoriented, roll out, climb to a safe altitude, find your references and the wind again, and start over. Pushing on is how altitude and airspeed quietly wander [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

check.q: What does fixating on the pylon cost you, according to the AFH?
check.a: The ability to judge rate; scan across several references instead [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

body.p: The AFH puts incorrect rudder use first, then lists nine more errors [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. Here they are with fixes.

head: AFH common error
Fix
rows: Rudder used to hold the pylon
Rudder for coordination only; fix the line with altitude [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Not clearing the area, initially and throughout
Clearing turns, spoken scan, look up at every straight leg [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Feel the seat and check the ball [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]
Excessive gain or loss of altitude
Small, early climbs and descents with power, not big chases [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]
Prominent, same elevation, 3 to 5 seconds apart, across the wind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]
Not entering the pylon turns into the wind
Diagonal entry to the downwind side of the first pylon [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Heading between pylons that does not correct for drift
Roll out with a wind correction angle [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Bank not timed so the turn is set with the pylon in position
Start the roll as the pylon nears the wingtip [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]
Unable to find the pivotal altitude
Compute it before flight, then fine-tune by watching the line [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]

body.p: Table source: the error list [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]; fixes as cited.

callout.text: Chasing the altimeter is its own error. The pylon tells you where pivotal altitude is; the altimeter does not [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].
Debrief each eight in one line: where did the pylon move, which way did I correct, and was the ball centered?

check.q: Name the error the AFH lists first for holding a pylon.
check.a: Incorrect use of the rudder to yaw the wing forward or back [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

Labels mark gaining altitude on the upper part of each loop, high groundspeed and high pivotal altitude near the bottom, and lowest groundspeed and lowest pivotal altitude on the far right side heading into the wind.

f2.caption: Figure 7-11. Line of sight. (AFH 7-15)
f2.alt: Two drawings of a high-wing airplane show the line of sight running parallel to the lateral axis, slightly ahead of the wing's leading edge. Two photos taken from the cockpit show a pond as the pylon: one labeled too high, pylon ahead, and one labeled too low, pylon behind.

f3.caption: Figure 7-12. Speed versus pivotal altitude. (AFH 7-15)
f3.alt: A table of groundspeed in knots and miles per hour against approximate pivotal altitude: 87 knots or 100 mph, 670; 91 or 105, 735; 96 or 110, 810; 100 or 115, 885; 104 or 120, 960; 109 or 125, 1050; 113 or 130, 1130.

f4.caption: Figure 7-13. Effect of different altitudes on line of sight. (AFH 7-16)
f4.alt: Three banked airplanes circle a tower pylon on three stacked rings labeled too high, pivotal altitude and too low. A sight line from each airplane runs to the ground: from the middle airplane it meets the pylon, from the top airplane it lands beyond the pylon, and from the bottom airplane it falls short of it.

f5.caption: Figure 7-14. Bank angle versus pivotal altitude. (AFH 7-17)
f5.alt: Side view of a tower pylon and three airplanes on one horizontal line marked pivotal altitude. Red sight lines run from each airplane along its lowered wing to the pylon. The airplane closest to the pylon is banked 60°, the middle one 45° and the farthest one 30°.

f6.caption: Figure 7-2. Effect of wind during a turn. (AFH 7-4)
f6.alt: Two airplanes make 180° turns from a road. On the left, with no wind, the ground path is a neat half circle. On the right, with a 20-knot wind blowing up the page, the actual ground path bulges wider and farther downwind than the dashed intended ground path.

scenario.title: Gusty checkride over flat farmland
scenario.setup: You are on your commercial checkride in a four-seat high-wing trainer. The wind at 1,000 feet is from the south at about 20 knots and gusty, and there is some haze. The practice area is flat farmland at 1,150 feet MSL with scattered grain bins, a cattle feedlot, and a crop duster that works the fields. The examiner asks for eights on pylons.

questions.q: You plan on about 100 knots groundspeed on the crosswind legs. What pivotal altitude do you brief, and how firmly do you hold it?
questions.a: 100 x 100 / 11.3 = 885 feet above the pylons, plus 1,150 = about 2,035 feet MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. It is a starting estimate; the pivotal altitude changes with groundspeed through each turn and is found by watching the sight line, not the altimeter [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

questions.q: The gusts make the sight line jump ahead and behind the pylon for a second or two at a time. How do you handle that?
questions.a: Small, temporary bank changes: shallow slightly to bring a lagging line forward, or steepen briefly to turn back a line that has moved ahead [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Keep the corrections smooth and continuous (ACS CA.V.E.S6).

questions.q: On the second pylon you notice the oil pressure needle near the bottom of the green. What now?
questions.a: This is why ground reference maneuvers include a regular scan of the engine instruments [[24:147|AFH 7-1]]. Roll out, climb if the engine allows, and head toward the landing spot you picked before entry; at low altitude there is little time or glide distance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

questions.q: The crop duster pops up low, below the horizon off your nose, as you roll out between pylons. What do you know and do?
questions.a: The AFH warns to look for other aircraft at low altitude [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Below the horizon means it is probably lower than you; if it shows no relative motion and grows, take evasive action [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]]. Haze makes it harder to see, so keep scanning after you react [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

questions.q: On the downwind side the pylon keeps sliding behind your sight line, and you catch yourself pushing inside rudder to drag the wing back. What is wrong?
questions.a: Using rudder to yaw the wing onto the pylon is the most common error; the rudder is for coordination only [[24:164|AFH 7-18]]. The pylon behind means you are low: climb [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. A slip or skid near the stall can start a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

questions.q: Climbing on the downwind side, the airspeed drops 8 knots. Why, and what is the fix?
questions.a: You traded airspeed for altitude without adding energy [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. The AFH has you add power to hold airspeed while you regain altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Less airspeed also means less stall margin [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

skills.do: Clear the area before entering, and keep clearing throughout the maneuver.
skills.practice: Fly two 90° clearing turns calling 'clear left, right, above, and below', and look up and out on every straight leg [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Tell the examiner an approximate pivotal altitude worked out from groundspeed and pylon elevation.
skills.practice: Before each lesson compute it for upwind, downwind and crosswind from the forecast wind, the sectional elevation and the POH maneuvering speed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

skills.do: Pick two pylons that permit straight-and-level flight between them.
skills.practice: Choose prominent pylons at the same elevation, across the wind, about 3 to 5 seconds of straight flight apart, away from people and livestock [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

skills.do: Enter in the correct direction and position at an appropriate altitude and airspeed.
skills.practice: Fly diagonally crosswind between the pylons to the downwind side of the first one so the first turn is into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Use the bank the conditions call for, never more than 40°.
skills.practice: Vary your entry distance with your CFI to learn which distance gives about 30° and which gives 40° at the steepest point [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

skills.do: Keep the line-of-sight reference on the pylon with smooth, continuous corrections.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call 'pylon ahead' or 'pylon behind' while you answer with a small descent or climb [[24:163|AFH 7-17]] [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

skills.do: Fly accurately and coordinated while your eyes are mostly outside on the pylons and the sky.
skills.practice: Practice a scan of pylon, horizon, ball and airspeed, and avoid fixating on the pylon [[24:147|AFH 7-1]].

skills.do: Hold the pylon with the right pivotal altitude, with no slips or skids.
skills.practice: Fly a full eight with your feet doing only coordination; any pylon drift gets an altitude fix [[24:164|AFH 7-18]] [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

quiz.why: The pivotal altitude is determined by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

quiz.q: With groundspeed in knots, the rule of thumb divides groundspeed squared by:
quiz.why: Divide by 11.3 for knots, or by 15 for miles per hour, then add the pylon's MSL elevation [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

quiz.q: The visual reference line runs from the pilot's eyes to the pylon and is parallel to:
quiz.why: The line from the pilot's eyes to the pylon stays parallel to the lateral axis [[24:160|AFH 7-14]].

quiz.q: How long should the straight-and-level leg between pylons last?
quiz.why: Pylon spacing should give a straight-and-level segment of 3 to 5 seconds [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: The two pylons should lie on a line that is:
quiz.why: Select two pylons along a line perpendicular to the wind [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

quiz.q: In which direction is the first pylon turn made?
options: Whichever way puts the sun behind you
quiz.why: Enter so the first turn is made into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: Turning on the pylon, your heading swings toward upwind. What should you expect to do?
options: Hold altitude and steepen the bank
quiz.why: Headed upwind, groundspeed decreases and so does the pivotal altitude, so descend [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

quiz.q: What is the commercial ACS bank limit for eights on pylons?
quiz.why: Establish the correct bank for the conditions, not to exceed 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5).

quiz.q: According to the AFH, what is the most common error in trying to hold a pylon?
options: Flying too far from the pylon
quiz.why: The most common error is incorrect rudder use to yaw the wing toward the pylon [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

quiz.q: What does the AFH say about correcting the pivotal altitude with the altimeter?
options: It works only in calm wind
It is required by the ACS
quiz.why: Attempting to correct pivotal altitude by using the altimeter is ineffective; use the apparent movement of the sight line [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: Groundspeed is 104 knots and the pylons sit at 900 feet MSL. About what should the altimeter read?
You are at pivotal altitude with 30° of bank. Your CFI wants 40° at the steepest point. What do you change?
options: Fly closer to the pylon; the pivotal altitude stays the same
final_quiz.why: Distance from the pylon sets the bank; the bank chosen does not change the pivotal altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: You start well above pivotal altitude in a medium-bank turn around the pylon, reduce power and descend at maneuvering speed. The sight line's backward drift across the ground slows, then stops for an instant. What does that tell you?
options: You are now below the pivotal altitude
You are at the pivotal altitude
final_quiz.why: The altitude where the sight line stops moving across the ground is the pivotal altitude; keep descending and the line starts to move forward, which means you are below it [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: A gust makes the sight line lag behind the pylon for a moment. What does the AFH suggest?
options: Reduce the bank slightly and fly nearly straight to bring the line forward
final_quiz.why: Temporary variations are fixed by reducing bank slightly to bring a lagging line forward, or increasing bank to turn back a line that has moved ahead [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

final_quiz.q: Your candidate pylons are a silo at 720 feet MSL and a water tank at 760 feet MSL. What is the problem?
options: You would need to climb or descend between each turn
Water tanks are not allowed as pylons
The pivotal altitude rule only works below 500 feet MSL
final_quiz.why: Pylons should be at the same elevation; differences of more than a few feet mean climbing or descending between turns [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: You are lighter today, and the POH maneuvering speed for your weight is lower. If you fly that lower speed, the pivotal altitude will be:
options: The same, because only bank matters
The same, because weight does not affect groundspeed
final_quiz.why: The POH gives maneuvering speeds by weight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Less airspeed means less groundspeed, and pivotal altitude is set by groundspeed [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your POH stall speed is 48 knots with the wings level. About what is it in a level turn at the 40° bank limit?
final_quiz.why: Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Application: at 40° the load factor is 1 / cos 40° = 1.31, its square root is 1.14, and 48 x 1.14 = 54.8, about 55 knots. 63 knots is the mistake of multiplying by the load factor itself. The AFH has you check the POH stall speed at the steepest bank you expect [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: On the downwind side you hold the bank with aileron and push inside rudder to swing the wing back to the pylon. If the airplane stalls, what is most likely?
options: No stall is possible below 40° of bank
A spin entry in the direction of the rudder
final_quiz.why: Skidding inside rudder with opposite aileron is a cross-control setup [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. A stall in a slipping or skidding turn can start a spin in the direction of the rudder [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

final_quiz.q: Which hazards does the AFH specifically tell you to look for during ground reference maneuvers?
options: Other aircraft including helicopters, and towers and wires
final_quiz.why: Look for other aircraft, including helicopters, and for obstructions such as radio towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

final_quiz.q: You climb toward the higher downwind pivotal altitude using pitch alone. What follows?
options: Airspeed falls, which also lowers groundspeed and the pivotal altitude you were chasing
The bank angle shallows by itself
final_quiz.why: Trading airspeed for altitude moves them in opposite directions unless thrust changes [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. The AFH adds power to hold airspeed while regaining altitude [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Lower groundspeed means a lower pivotal altitude [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

final_quiz.q: Why not pick pylons so far apart that the straight leg lasts 30 seconds?
options: It makes the pivotal altitude higher
It adds unnecessary straight-and-level flight between turns
final_quiz.why: Pylons should give time to plan the turns but not be so far apart that they cause unnecessary straight-and-level flight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner sees you hold the pylon perfectly, but with the ball off center in a skid. Which ACS element is not met?
options: CA.V.E.S8, maintain pylon position avoiding slips and skids
final_quiz.why: S8 asks you to maintain pylon position using appropriate pivotal altitude, avoiding slips and skids (ACS CA.V.E.S8). AFH says to use the rudder only for coordination and lists skidding or slipping in turns as an error [[24:164|AFH 7-18]].

final_quiz.q: The wind is from the north and your pylons lie east and west of each other. You roll out of the first pylon turn. Where are you aiming?
options: A point north of the second pylon
A point on the line between the pylons, just short of the second
A point south of the second pylon, as far from it as you started from the first
final_quiz.why: Roll out with a wind correction angle and fly diagonally to a point downwind of the second pylon, equal in distance to where you started from the first [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. With a north wind, downwind is south.

takeaways: Pivotal altitude: groundspeed squared over 11.3 (knots) or 15 (mph), plus the pylon's elevation.
Groundspeed sets the pivotal altitude. Bank does not; your distance from the pylon sets the bank.
Pylon runs ahead: too high, descend. Pylon falls behind: too low, climb.
Pylons: prominent, same elevation, across the wind, 3 to 5 seconds apart, away from people and livestock.
Enter diagonally to the downwind side, first turn into the wind; descend going upwind, climb going downwind.
Rudder is only for coordination. Never yaw the wing onto the pylon, and keep the bank at or under 40°.
Low and turning: clear the area, watch for towers and helicopters, manage energy with power, and keep a field picked.
cfi_notes: The AFH says the pivotal altitude varies 'slightly' through the turn [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Application: the rule of thumb at 100 knots TAS in a 15-knot wind gives about 639 feet straight upwind, 865 crosswind and 1,170 straight downwind. You never fly the pylon turn straight downwind, so the real spread is smaller, but in strong wind expect climbs and descents of a few hundred feet, not small ones.

AFH 7-14 says the wingtip is not the correct reference [[24:160|AFH 7-14]], yet AFH 7-17 starts the turn when the pylon is 'just ahead of the wingtip' [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. Teach the wingtip only as the cue to roll in; while turning, the reference is the eye-level line parallel to the lateral axis.

The AFH entry is 'diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind from the first pylon' [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. The popular '45° to the downwind' wording is instructor technique; the 45° figure is not in the AFH text. Do not mix it up with eights around pylons, which starts on a downwind heading midway between the pylons [[24:159|AFH 7-13]].

Bank limits differ by source: the ACS caps it at 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5), AFH 7-2 gives 45° as a general ground reference limit [[24:148|AFH 7-2]], and Figure 7-14 shows 60° [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. On the checkride 40° governs.

Figure 7-12's numbers are heights above the pylon, not altimeter readings, and are rounded. Some rows match the knots rule (87, 100, 109 and 113 knots) and others the mph rule (105, 110 and 120 mph); the two rules never differ by more than about 6 feet on the table. Example: 96 knots gives 816 by the knots rule, 110 mph gives 807 by the mph rule, and the table shows 810 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].
The 'ahead/behind' wording is easy to reverse under stress. Teach it from the Figure 7-11 photos first: too high, pylon ahead; too low, pylon behind [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

The 11.3 derivation in this lesson comes from the PHAK radius formula, which uses true airspeed [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]], with groundspeed swapped in. It explains the rule of thumb; it is not an FAA derivation.

Students often climb and descend with pitch only. Use the AFH demonstration (reduce power to descend, add power to climb at maneuvering speed) [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] and the energy model [[24:88|AFH 4-2]] to show why airspeed, groundspeed and pivotal altitude then wander together.
gaps: The ACS gives no altitude or airspeed tolerances for this Task, only the 40° bank limit (ACS CA.V.E.S5). How much pylon wander is acceptable is the evaluator's judgment.
The entry airspeed comes from the POH/AFM. The AFH uses maneuvering speed in its demonstration [[24:162|AFH 7-16]] but gives no single number.
No source here describes how to end the maneuver, though the ACS asks about the phases from entry to recovery (ACS CA.V.E.K5). Agree on a recovery with your CFI.
The sources do not say how far from the pylon to fly for a given bank in your airplane; Figure 7-14 only shows that closer means steeper [[24:163|AFH 7-17]]. That comes from practice.

No source gives a minimum altitude for this Task beyond the general 600 to 1,000 feet AGL and obstacle clearance [[24:148|AFH 7-2]] and 14 CFR 91.119 [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]]. In a fast airplane the pivotal altitude may sit above that range.

activities.title: Find the sight lines
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the figure.

pins.label: Sight line at pivotal altitude: meets the pylon
Sight line from above pivotal altitude: lands beyond the pylon
Sight line from below pivotal altitude: falls short of the pylon

activities.title: Climb or descend?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap what you should do.

items.t: The pylon appears to move back, behind your sight line
The pylon appears to move ahead of your sight line
Your heading swings from crosswind toward downwind and groundspeed builds
The altimeter shows your computed pivotal altitude, but the pylon keeps moving ahead of your sight line
The projected sight line creeps forward along the ground
The projected sight line slides backward across the ground

activities.title: Work the pivotal altitude
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Groundspeed 95 knots. The pylons are at 620 feet MSL. What should the altimeter read (feet MSL)?
Groundspeed 120 mph. Using the mph rule, how high above the pylon is the pivotal altitude?
items.why: 120 x 120 = 14,400. 14,400 / 15 = 960 feet, the same as the 120 mph row in Figure 7-12 [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

items.q: You want the pivotal altitude to be 1,000 feet above the pylon. What groundspeed in knots gives that?
items.why: Groundspeed squared = 1,000 x 11.3 = 11,300. Square root of 11,300 = 106.3 knots [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

items.q: 100 knots TAS, 15-knot wind. Heading straight upwind, how high above the pylon is the pivotal altitude?
Same airplane and wind, heading straight downwind. How much higher is the pivotal altitude than heading upwind?
Application of Figure 7-14: at 885 feet above the pylon, how far from it (feet) must you be for exactly 40° of bank?
items.why: Application: the sight line runs along the lateral axis, so tan(bank) = height / distance. Distance = 885 / tan 40° = 885 / 0.8391 = 1,054.7 feet. Closer than that, the bank passes the 40° limit (ACS CA.V.E.S5) [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

activities.title: True or false: pylons and wind
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The rule of thumb gives height above the pylon, so you add the pylon's MSL elevation.
cards.why: True. Square the groundspeed, divide, then add the MSL altitude of the ground reference [[24:161|AFH 7-15]].

cards.s: Steepening the bank lowers the pivotal altitude.
cards.why: False. The bank chosen does not alter the pivotal altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

cards.s: In eights on pylons you must hold a constant radius around each pylon.
cards.why: False. The turn does not have to be a constant radius, so no drift correction is needed in the turn [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

cards.s: Between the pylons you roll out with a wind correction angle.
cards.why: True. Complete the rollout with the proper wind correction angle to correct for drift [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

cards.s: A pylon next to a herd of cattle is a good choice because it is easy to spot.
cards.why: False. The maneuver area should be well away from herds of livestock [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

cards.s: Ground reference maneuvers are generally flown between 600 and 1,000 feet AGL.
cards.why: True [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Your pivotal altitude may fall above or below that, so check obstacle clearance and 14 CFR 91.119 [[60:449|14 CFR 91.119]].

cards.s: A 10-knot crosswind drifts a 180-knot airplane half as far per hour as a 90-knot airplane.
cards.why: False. Both drift 10 nautical miles every hour; speed does not change the drift rate [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

activities.title: Put the eight in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Estimate the pivotal altitudes on the ground from wind, pylon elevation and maneuvering speed
Announce on the practice frequency and make two 90° clearing turns
Fly diagonally crosswind between the pylons toward a point downwind of the first pylon
As the pylon nears the wingtip, roll in until the sight line rests on the pylon
Descend as you turn upwind and groundspeed falls; climb as groundspeed builds again
Roll out toward downwind with a wind correction angle, aiming downwind of the second pylon
Roll into the opposite turn around the second pylon

activities.title: Match the hazard to the defense
activities.intro: Tap a hazard, then the defense that fits it.

pairs.l: Pylon drifting and the urge to push rudder
pairs.r: Rudder only for coordination; fix the line with altitude

pairs.l: Towers and wires near the pylons
pairs.r: At least 500 feet vertical and 2,000 feet horizontal clearance

pairs.l: Airspeed bleeding off in the climb to pivotal altitude
pairs.r: Add power to hold airspeed while climbing

pairs.l: Bank getting too steep close to the pylon
pairs.r: Exit and set up again farther from the reference

activities.title: Eights on pylons, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are flying a high-wing trainer with your CFI to practice for the commercial checkride. The wind at 1,000 feet is from the west at 15 knots. The farmland below is flat at about 700 feet MSL, and you are light today.

steps.s: Your CFI says 'Pick your pylons.' Which pair do you choose?
options: A farmhouse and a lone tree about two miles apart
Two grain bins on an east-west line, about 5 seconds apart
Two grain bins on a north-south line, about 5 seconds of straight flight apart, same ground level, away from houses and livestock
A radio tower and a barn on a ridge
steps.why: With a west wind, a north-south line is perpendicular to the wind; pylons should be prominent, the same elevation and 3 to 5 seconds apart [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Stay away from people, livestock, towers and wires [[24:148|AFH 7-2]].

steps.s: The POH maneuvering speed for your weight is 95 knots, and you treat that as your crosswind groundspeed. What altimeter target do you brief?
steps.why: 95 x 95 = 9,025. 9,025 / 11.3 = 799 feet above the pylons. 799 + 700 = 1,499, about 1,500 feet MSL [[24:161|AFH 7-15]]. The POH gives maneuvering speeds by weight [[24:162|AFH 7-16]].

steps.s: Clearing turns are done. How do you enter?
options: Come in from the upwind side so the first turn is downwind
Fly straight upwind over the first pylon
Fly diagonally crosswind between the pylons to the downwind (east) side of the first pylon
Fly directly over the midpoint heading west
steps.why: Enter diagonally crosswind between the pylons to a point downwind of the first pylon so the first turn is into the wind [[24:163|AFH 7-17]].

steps.s: Heading into the wind on the first pylon, the pylon slides back, behind your sight line.
options: Push inside rudder to swing the wing back
Descend more, since you are heading upwind
Climb a little, adding power to hold airspeed
steps.why: Pylon moving back means the sight line is ahead of it: you are low, so increase altitude [[24:163|AFH 7-17]], with power to hold airspeed [[24:162|AFH 7-16]]. Rudder is for coordination only [[24:164|AFH 7-18]], and the bank limit is 40° (ACS CA.V.E.S5).

steps.s: On the second pylon, about 800 feet above the ground, the engine starts running rough.
options: Roll out, set best glide, head for the field you picked and plan to land toward the west
Keep flying the eight while you troubleshoot
Turn east with the wind to reach a farther, nicer field
Pull up hard to gain altitude
steps.why: Low altitude means little time and glide distance, so landing spots are chosen before you start [[24:148|AFH 7-2]]. Set best glide speed [[24:199|AFH 9-28]]. Landing into the wind lowers groundspeed, and doubling groundspeed means four times the destructive energy [[24:352|AFH 18-3]].
